asDecan.p: Each sign is split into three slices of ten degrees, the decans, and each slice gets a planet and a small card of its own. Your Sun is somewhere from 20 to 29 degrees of Taurus, the last stretch of the sign, and in the Chaldean order Saturn takes that slice. Saturn has no special dignity in Taurus. It's a guest there, neither helped nor held back, so it picks up the colour of Venus, who rules the sign. That's an odd pairing when you think about it, the planet of time and limits sitting inside the sign of comfort and good food. The Five of Pentacles, Mercury's slice, opens Taurus worried about being left out in the cold. The Six, the Moon's slice, is about giving and receiving. Yours comes last, when the sign is ripe and already leaning toward Gemini, and it's the one that stops to count. The Hierophant is your Sun card, and this is the finer grain inside it.

You're the person at a family dinner who asks your cousin how the business is actually going, and then wants numbers. You check on a savings account the way other people check the weather. When a friend sends a photo of their new sourdough starter, you're already wondering whether they'll keep it alive past March. A Sunday with nothing planned usually ends up in the garden or at the kitchen bench, doing something with your hands that leaves a result you can look at later. Venus gives you a real taste for the good things, a decent coat, a proper chair. Saturn makes you want to know what they'll be like in ten years before you pay for them. So you'll stand in a shop for twenty minutes over one purchase, and then keep it for two decades.

Everyone knows you can wait. What's less obvious is that Saturn in these degrees also gives you a sharp eye for what isn't growing, and the nerve to say so. When a friend has been pouring money into a café for three years, you're the one who can sit with them over the books and say, kindly, that it's the lease that's sinking it, and they'll hear it from you. At work you're good at the annual review, the kind where somebody actually looks at what a project cost and what it gave back. You don't get dramatic about it. You just count what's on the vine, and people trust your count because they know how much you hate waste.

The shadow that's harder to spot is the private ledger. You don't mean to keep one, but you know who drove to the airport last time, whose turn it is to host Christmas, how many years you've carried a particular friendship without much coming back. Saturn is the planet that measures, and in a Venus sign it ends up measuring affection. Most of the time the ledger stays in a drawer. Then one evening your sister cancels for the third time and the whole account comes out at once, going back to 2009, and she has no idea where it came from. There's a quieter version too. You can be slow to start anything whose payoff you can't picture, so the evening class, the odd little side project, the trip with no plan, often never happen.

When something goes wrong, a redundancy, bad news about a parent's health, a relationship ending after years, your first move is to go very still. You eat the same meals, keep the same hours, water the plants, and look almost unbothered to anyone watching. Taurus does steadiness under fire well. A week or so later the stillness has gone heavy. You're replaying every year you put into the thing that failed and adding up what it cost, and Saturn is very good at that arithmetic. You stop replying to messages without meaning to. People close to you find this hard, because you look fine and you won't be hurried into talking. What helps is something physical with a short, visible result, like painting a fence, cooking a big meal for people, pulling out a garden bed. It gets you out of the long sum.

The Hierophant is your Sun card, so you're fairly traditional about love, and this slice adds Saturn's habit of checking how things are going. It surprises partners. Every so often, usually around an anniversary or a birthday, you want to talk about the relationship itself, what's working, what's gone stale, whether the plan for the house still makes sense. To you that's care. To someone who doesn't know you well it can feel like a performance review. Venus gives you plenty of warmth and a real appetite for touch, good food and slow evenings in, and you show love by keeping things running, the car serviced, the good sheets washed and back on the bed. You do best with someone who answers the check-in honestly and doesn't hear it as a threat.

Work that pays off late suits you. Vineyards and orchards, obviously, but also funds management, building up a physio practice over fifteen years, restoring old furniture, teaching the same subject until you're the person everyone rings. The Five of Pentacles people start out worried about scraping by, and the Six are busy sharing out what comes in. You're the one who knows the three-year numbers by heart. Saturn gives you stamina for the dull middle part of a project that other people drift away from. What tends to go wrong is the end. You grow the account, the client list, the team, and then somebody better at talking in meetings takes the credit, and you let it go because making a fuss feels cheap. When the harvest comes in, ask for your share of it in writing.

At twenty this decan can feel stuck, to be honest. Friends are moving cities, changing courses, trying things, and you're still in the same part-time job because you want to see where it goes, and you worry you're behind. By the mid-thirties the picture tends to flip. Things you started quietly ten years earlier, a savings habit, a skill, a friendship, a small business, have grown into something solid, and people start asking how you did it. That's usually also when the private ledger costs you something, a friend lost over an old account nobody else remembered. These degrees sit at the very end of Taurus, leaning toward Gemini, and the fifties often bring that out. People with this decan get curious again, take up an instrument, go back to study for no return at all, and seem to enjoy it.

Plant something from seed, a tomato, a lemon tree, a pot of basil on the windowsill, and keep a scrap of paper next to it. Every time you water it, write down one thing in your own life you're waiting on, and underneath, one honest line about whether it's growing. Don't decide anything yet. When the plant either fruits or dies, read the whole list back and cross off anything you've written down five times without a single change in the second line.
